body: A Markov semigroup is hypercontractive if $\|P_tf\|_q\le\|f\|_p$ whenever $q-1\le e^{2t/C}(p-1)$; for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup (Nelson) and the noise operator on the cube (Bonami) $C=1$, and hypercontractivity is equivalent to a log-Sobolev inequality (Gross).

body:
Let f : {-1,1}^n -> R with the uniform product measure and let Delta_i f (x) = ( f(x) - f(x^{(i)}) ) / 2, where x^{(i)} flips coordinate i. Then there is a UNIVERSAL constant C with Var(f) <= C sum_{i=1}^n || Delta_i f ||_2^2 / ( 1 + log( || Delta_i f ||_2 / || Delta_i f ||_1 ) ), with the convention that a term is 0 when Delta_i f = 0. The unimproved bound Var(f) <= sum_i ||Delta_i f||_2^2 is the Efron-Stein inequality on the cube; Talagrand's refinement gains a LOGARITHMIC factor for every coordinate whose influence is spread out, that is whose L2 and L1 norms are far apart, and gains nothing for a coordinate whose discrete derivative is essentially an indicator. This is precisely the inequality Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm apply to first-passage percolation with two-valued weights to obtain Var <= C n / log n, and the reason their theorem carries a two-point weight hypothesis is that the L1-L2 comparison must be run on that specific cube structure. The p-biased and Gaussian analogues exist with modified constants; the Gaussian version replaces the log ratio by an entropy term (Falik-Samorodnitsky). [Talagrand (1994), 'On Russo's approximate zero-one law', Ann. Probab. 22; used in Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm (2003)]
uniform product measure on the discrete cube {-1,1}^n
f real-valued and square integrable on the cube
C is a universal constant, in particular independent of n and of f

body:
Let f : {-1,1}^n -> R with the uniform measure, with Fourier-Walsh expansion f = sum_{S subset [n]} fhat(S) chi_S where chi_S(x) = prod_{i in S} x_i. For 0 <= rho <= 1 define the noise operator T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} fhat(S) chi_S. Then for all 1 <= p <= q < infinity, || T_rho f ||_q <= || f ||_p whenever rho <= sqrt( (p-1)/(q-1) ). Two standard specialisations: taking p = 2 gives || T_rho f ||_q <= || f ||_2 for rho = 1/sqrt(q-1); and for f of DEGREE at most d, meaning fhat(S) = 0 whenever |S| > d, one gets || f ||_q <= (q-1)^{d/2} || f ||_2 for every q >= 2, and by duality || f ||_2 <= (q-1)^{d/2} ||f||_{q'} for the conjugate exponent. The degree-d moment comparison is the workhorse: it says low-degree functions on the cube have all L^q norms comparable to their L^2 norm with a constant depending only on the degree and q, not on n, which is exactly the dimension-free input that KKL and Talagrand's variance inequality consume. The measure must be the UNIFORM (or a fixed p-biased, with a different constant) product measure - the theorem is about product measures on the cube. [Bonami (1970), Beckner (1975); see O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, Chapter 9]
the uniform product measure on {-1,1}^n
1 <= p <= q < infinity and 0 <= rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1))
the constant is independent of n

Normalising a = 1 and expanding both sides as power series in b, one compares coefficients termwise; the inequality reduces to the elementary fact that the binomial-type coefficients of (1 + rho b)^q + (1 - rho b)^q are dominated by those coming from the p-side under the stated constraint on rho, which is checked directly for the first two orders and follows for the rest from the same constraint. STEP 2, tensorization: the hypercontractive constant of a product is the minimum of the constants of the factors. Precisely, if T_rho is a contraction from L^p to L^q on each factor space then it is a contraction from L^p to L^q on the product. This is proved by applying the one-dimensional bound in one coordinate at a time and using Minkowski's integral inequality, valid because q >= p, to exchange the order of the L^q norm in the remaining coordinates with the L^p norm in the coordinate being processed. If g is a standard Gaussian vector in R^n and f : R^n -> R is L-Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean norm, then P(|f(g) - E f(g)| > t) <= 2 exp(-t^2 / (2 L^2)) for all t > 0. An analogous inequality, with adjusted constants, holds for the uniform measure on the sphere; this isoperimetric concentration underlies laws of robustness.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Efron-Stein: for f(X_1,...,X_n) with independent coordinates, Var f <= (1/2) sum_i E[(f(X) - f(X^{(i)}))^2], where X^{(i)} resamples coordinate i; for a Boolean function under a product measure the right side is a constant times the total influence sum_i I_i(f). This bounds variance by total influence and needs no monotonicity. Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm (1999): if f_n : {0,1}^{m_n} -> {0,1} satisfy sum_i I_i(f_n)^2 -> 0 then (f_n) is noise sensitive, i.e. Cov(f_n(omega), f_n(omega^eps)) -> 0 for every fixed noise level eps > 0; for monotone functions the converse also holds. The quantitative engine is Talagrand's inequality Var f <= C sum_i I_i(f)/log(e/I_i(f)) (hypercontractivity), which for functions with all influences at most n^{-a} improves Efron-Stein by a factor log n; the same mechanism gives the BKS sublinear variance bound Var(first-passage time to distance n) <= C n/log n for first-passage percolation with suitable edge weights. What these do NOT give: a lower bound on any individual influence (that is Kahn-Kalai-Linial: max_i I_i >= c Var(f) log n / n), or a power improvement n^{1-eps} on the variance, which remains open outside integrable models. Typical failure: Using the plain Efron-Stein variance bound and mistaking it for the BKS lower bound on the maximal individual influence, which is a distinct and much sharper statement requiring monotonicity and a total-influence hypothesis; conflating the two leads to claiming individual-coordinate sensitivity conclusions, needed for noise-sensitivity theorems, from a tool that in its basic form only controls the aggregate variance. Canonical reference: Efron and Stein, 1981, The Annals of Statistics; Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm, 1999, Publications Mathematiques de l'IHES.
Independent coordinates (product measure)
BKS noise sensitivity criterion: sum of squared influences tends to zero
Talagrand's logarithmic improvement needs hypercontractivity of the product measure

Let E be a Banach space and v_1, ..., v_n in E. Let eps_1, ..., eps_n be independent Rademacher random variables. Then for any 1 <= p < q < infinity, there exists a constant C_{p, q} > 0 depending only on p and q such that ( E[ || sum_{i=1}^n eps_i * v_i ||_E^q ] )^{1/q} <= C_{p, q} * ( E[ || sum_{i=1}^n eps_i * v_i ||_E^p ] )^{1/p}.

Let 1 <= p, q < infinity and rho in [0, 1]. If |E[a(X) b(Y)]| <= ||a||_p ||b||_q for all real a, b on one bit under the rho-correlated pair, then |E[f(X) g(Y)]| <= ||f||_p ||g||_q for all real f, g on {-1, 1}^n when the n coordinate pairs are independent copies of that pair. The product structure of the coupling is needed: on two uniform bits let Y = (X_2, X_1); each pair (X_i, Y_i) is an independent uniform pair (the rho = 0 law), but for A = {x_1 = x_2} and f = g = 1_A, E[f(X) g(Y)] = 1/2 while ||f||_1 ||g||_1 = 1/4.

body: Let gamma be the standard Gaussian measure on R^n. The ORNSTEIN-UHLENBECK SEMIGROUP is defined by MEHLER'S FORMULA P_t f(x) = integral f( e^{-t} x + sqrt(1 - e^{-2t}) y ) gamma(dy) for t >= 0. It is a Markov semigroup: P_0 = identity, P_{s+t} = P_s P_t, P_t 1 = 1, P_t preserves nonnegativity, gamma is INVARIANT (integral P_t f dgamma = integral f dgamma), and P_t is SELF-ADJOINT on L^2(gamma). Its generator is L f = Laplacian f - x . grad f, which satisfies the integration-by-parts identity integral (L u) v dgamma = - integral grad u . grad v dgamma. The Hermite polynomials diagonalise it: L He_alpha = - |alpha| He_alpha and P_t He_alpha = e^{-|alpha| t} He_alpha, so the n-th Wiener chaos is the eigenspace of eigenvalue -n. The COMMUTATION RELATION grad P_t f = e^{-t} P_t grad f follows by differentiating Mehler's formula under the integral. Two facts to keep straight: this is the semigroup for the standard Gaussian, and other normalisations of the generator (for example Laplacian/2 minus x . grad/2) rescale time and change the constants in the associated Poincare and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. As t -> infinity, P_t f -> integral f dgamma, and the exponential rate of that convergence in L^2 is exactly 1, the spectral gap, which is the Gaussian Poincare inequality. [standard; e.g. Bakry, Gentil and Ledoux, Analysis and Geometry of Markov Diffusion Operators, Section 2.7]

Let f: {0, 1}^n -> {0, 1}, n >= 2, under the uniform measure, q_j(f) = P(f(X) != f(X with bit j flipped)) and I_flip(f) = sum_j q_j(f). Fix a coordinate i and let f_0, f_1 be the restrictions x_i = 0, 1 on the remaining (n - 1)-cube. Then q_j(f) = (q_j(f_0) + q_j(f_1))/2 for j != i, q_i(f) = E[(f_1 - f_0)^2], and so I_flip(f) = q_i(f) + (I_flip(f_0) + I_flip(f_1))/2. Also Var(f) = (Var f_0 + Var f_1)/2 + (a_1 - a_0)^2/4 with a_b = E f_b, and the Poincare defect D(f) = I_flip(f) - 4 Var(f) satisfies D(f) = (D(f_0) + D(f_1))/2 + Var(f_1 - f_0).

Let (X, Y) be uniform on {-1, 1}^n x {-1, 1}^n with independent coordinate pairs and E[X_i Y_i] = rho, and let r, s >= 0 with rho^2 <= rs <= 1. Then |E[f(X) g(Y)]| <= ||f||_{1+r} ||g||_{1+s} for all real f, g. For s > 0 this two-function bound is equivalent to the one-function bound ||T_rho f||_{(1+s)/s} <= ||f||_{1+r}, and with p = 1 + r, q = (1 + s)/s the condition rho^2 <= rs is rho^2 <= (p - 1)/(q - 1). Conversely, if the bound holds for all f, g on one bit with r, s > 0, then rho^2 <= rs.

body:
Let gamma be the standard Gaussian measure on R^n. For every locally Lipschitz f with f and grad f in L^2(gamma), Ent_gamma(f^2) <= 2 E_gamma[ |grad f|^2 ], where Ent(g) = E[g log g] - E[g] log E[g] for g >= 0. The constant 2 is sharp, with near-equality for exponentials f = e^{a . x / 2}. As with the Poincare inequality the constant is DIMENSION-FREE, obtained from the one-dimensional case by tensorization of entropy. Gross's theorem states that this inequality is EQUIVALENT to Nelson's hypercontractivity for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, and it implies the Gaussian Poincare inequality by linearisation. Combined with the Herbst argument it yields Gaussian concentration for Lipschitz functions with the sharp sub-Gaussian variance proxy equal to the square of the Lipschitz constant. Care with normalisation: the inequality is often written as Ent(f) <= 2 E[ |grad sqrt(f)|^2 ] for f >= 0, which is the same statement after substituting f -> f^2, and some sources carry a factor 1/2 from using a different generator normalisation; the version stated here is the one matching the standard Gaussian and the generator L = Laplacian minus x . gradient. [Gross (1975); see Bakry, Gentil and Ledoux, Analysis and Geometry of Markov Diffusion Operators, Chapter 5]

Let (P_t) be the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup with P_t g(x) = E[ g(e^{-t} x + sqrt(1 - e^{-2t}) Z) ] for Z standard Gaussian, which is symmetric in L^2(gamma) with invariant measure gamma, has generator L g = Laplacian g minus x . grad g, and satisfies the commutation relation grad P_t g = e^{-t} P_t grad g directly from the formula by differentiating under the expectation. Put g = f^2 >= 0 and consider Phi(t) = E[ P_t g log P_t g ]. Since P_0 g = g and P_infinity g = E[g], one has Ent(g) = Phi(0) - Phi(infinity) = - integral_0^infinity Phi'(t) dt. Differentiating and integrating by parts against the invariant measure, Phi'(t) = E[ (L P_t g)(1 + log P_t g) ] = - E[ |grad P_t g|^2 / P_t g ], the last step using the integration-by-parts identity E[ (L u) v ] = - E[ grad u . grad v ] for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck generator. Hence Ent(g) = integral_0^infinity E[ |grad P_t g|^2 / P_t g ] dt. Apply the commutation relation and then the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the probability kernel P_t in the form |P_t (grad g)|^2 = |P_t (2 f grad f)|^2 <= 4 P_t(f^2) P_t(|grad f|^2) = 4 (P_t g) P_t(|grad f|^2). This gives E[ |grad P_t g|^2/P_t g ] <= 4 e^{-2t} E[ P_t(|grad f|^2) ] = 4 e^{-2t} E[ |grad f|^2 ] by invariance of gamma under P_t. title: Talagrand's L_1 - L_2 Influence Inequality

body:
On one uniform bit x in {-1, 1}, let 1 < p < q < infinity, rho in [-1, 1], T_rho the noise operator (T_rho x = rho x) and f_eps = 1 + eps x. Then log(||T_rho f_eps||_q/||f_eps||_p) = ((q - 1) rho^2 - (p - 1)) eps^2/2 + ((p - 1)(p^2 + p - 3) - (q - 1)(q^2 + q - 3) rho^4) eps^4/12 + O(eps^6) as eps -> 0. So if rho^2 > (p - 1)/(q - 1), small eps != 0 give ||T_rho f||_q > ||f||_p; if rho^2 < (p - 1)/(q - 1) the ratio is below 1 to second order; and at rho^2 = (p - 1)/(q - 1) the quartic coefficient equals (p - 1)(p - q)(pq - p - q + 2)/(12 (q - 1)) < 0, a strict local contraction.
